1.open: What is a chore or task that never seems to end, no matter how often you do it?
questions: The Teacher opens with "Futility of futilities! Everything is futile!" (v. 2). When have you felt that way, even for a moment? What was going on?
In verse 3 he asks, "What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?" What do you hope your work or effort will gain you? Is that hope holding up?
Verses 4 to 7 describe the sun, the wind and the rivers going round and round. What ordinary routines in your own life feel like that?
Verse 8 says "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing." Where do you notice that you always want a little more, whether it is news, things, or experiences?
Verse 11 says people of the past are not remembered. How does it feel to think you may be forgotten one day? Does it change what you want to build or leave behind?
The Teacher says he used wisdom to explore "all that is done under heaven" and called it "a pursuit of the wind" (vv. 13, 14). Why might a person who searches this hard end up so discouraged?
Verse 18 says "with much wisdom comes much sorrow." Have you found that knowing more can make life heavier? Where have you seen that?

Christians differ on whether this bleak voice is the book's final word or an honest voice of doubt that the rest of the book answers. Which one do you lean toward as you listen, and what would you want to find out as we keep reading?
1.life: This week, pick one task that feels repetitive or pointless and do it slowly, telling God plainly how you feel about it. Notice whether anything shifts, even a little.
1.prayer: Thank God that we can bring our tiredness and our doubts to him honestly. Ask him to show each person where their work and rest really matter.
1.tip: Some people may be uncomfortable that a Bible book sounds this hopeless, and others may be going through exactly that. Don't rush to cheer anyone up or fix the mood. Let the Teacher's honesty give people permission to be honest too, and remind the group that the book does not end here.

2.open: What is something you worked hard to get, and how did you feel a month after you got it?
questions: The Teacher says, "I will test you with pleasure," and then reports, "it proved to be futile" (v. 1). Why do you think fun and comfort, taken alone, leave people feeling empty?
In verses 4 to 8 he lists houses, vineyards, gardens, servants, herds and gold. If you made a list like that for our culture, what would be on it?

He says, "I refused my heart no pleasure," and yet he found "nothing to be gained under the sun" (vv. 10, 11). Which part of that surprises you more, that he had everything or that it still wasn't enough?

He says "wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness," but then adds that "one fate overcomes them both" (vv. 13, 14). What do you make of a writer who says wisdom matters and also says it cannot save us from death?

He says, "I hated all for which I had toiled," because he must leave it to someone else (v. 18). Who will inherit what you are working on now, whether that is a job, a home, a family or a church? How does that sit with you?
Verse 23 says that "even at night, his mind does not rest." Where does work or worry follow you into the night? Be as honest as you can, including if you are not sure any of this helps.

In verses 24 to 26 he says that eating, drinking and enjoying work are "from the hand of God." What is one ordinary good thing you could receive this week as a gift instead of something you have earned?
If wise and foolish people alike are eventually forgotten, what, if anything, makes your own efforts feel worth it to you?
2.life: Pick one ordinary moment this week, like a meal, a walk or a coffee with a friend. Slow down, enjoy it on purpose, and thank God for it as a gift.
2.prayer: Tell God honestly where your work or your pleasures have left you empty. Ask him to teach you to receive each day as a gift from his hand.
2.tip: Verses 24 to 26 can sound either cheerful or tired, and Christians read them both ways. Don't force a single answer. Let people say which tone they hear, and make room for anyone who finds the whole chapter bleak.

3.open: Which season of the year do you like best, and what do you usually find yourself doing in it?
questions: The writer begins, "To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven" (v. 1). Which pair in verses 2 to 8 matches the season of life you are in right now?
The list includes hard things like "a time to kill" and "a time to hate" (v. 3, v. 8). The point does not seem to be that each of these is good. What do you think he is saying about how life moves?
In verse 9 he asks, "What does the worker gain from his toil?" When have you worked hard and wondered what it was all for?

Verse 11 says God "has made everything beautiful in its time." Can you think of something painful that, looking back, you can now see differently? Or something that still does not look beautiful to you?

Verse 11 also says God "has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end." What do you make of wanting more than we can see or understand?
In verses 12 and 13 the writer says to "rejoice and do good" and to "find satisfaction in all his labor." He calls this "the gift of God." What ordinary gift in your week is easy to rush past?
In verse 16 he sees "wickedness" even in the place of judgment. How do you respond when you see injustice go unanswered, and what does verse 17 offer you?
In verse 21 he asks, "Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward?" Is there a question about God, death or the future that you are honestly unsure about? Say as much or as little as you like.
3.life: Pick one ordinary gift this week, like a meal, a walk or a task at work, and slow down to enjoy it on purpose. Thank God for it as a gift, not just something to get through.
3.prayer: Thank God that our times are in his hands even when we cannot see the whole picture. Ask for help to trust him in the season you are in, and to be honest with him about what you do not understand.
3.tip: Verses 18 to 21 sound bleak, and Christians read them differently: some hear the writer's real doubt left open, others hear a view he raises in order to answer with hope in God's judgment. Say that plainly, do not try to settle it, and let a doubting person say honestly where they are without hurrying to fix it.

4.open: Who is someone who has shown up for you when you really needed help, and what did they do?
questions: The writer sees "the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter" (v. 1). Where do you see people today who are hurting with no one beside them?
He says the dead are better off than the living, and better still are those who were never born (vv. 2-3). Why do you think the Bible includes such a bleak thought without softening it?

Verse 4 says success can spring from "a man's envy of his neighbor." Readers take this as either envy driving our hard work or success making us envied. How have you seen envy shape work, school or social media?
Verse 6 says, "Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind." What would "one handful with tranquility" look like in your own life right now?
The man in verses 7 and 8 asks, "For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?" When you look at what you work hardest for, who or what is it really for?
Verse 10 says, "if one falls down, his companion can lift him up." Tell about a time someone lifted you, or a time you wished someone had. What made it hard to ask for help?
Verse 16 ends by saying even a beloved new ruler is forgotten by those who come later. What does that say about chasing applause, and what seems worth chasing instead?

Christians differ on whether the bleak lines in this chapter are the writer's settled view or a limited view of life "under the sun" that the book means to challenge. Which part of the chapter feels most honest to you, and which part feels hardest to accept?
4.life: Pick one person this week and reach out to them with a call, a meal or an honest conversation. If you are the one who is struggling, let one person know and ask for help.
4.prayer: Thank God for the people who have lifted you up. Ask him to show you who is weeping with no comforter and to make you willing to sit with them.
4.tip: Verses 2 and 3 can sound shocking, and someone in the room may be carrying real despair. Don't rush to fix it or explain it away. Let the group sit with the honesty of the text, say that the Bible allows people to speak plainly about pain, and be ready to check in privately with anyone who seems to be struggling.

5.open: What is something small you have bought or been given that you enjoyed more than you expected?
questions: The Teacher begins, "Guard your steps when you go to the house of God" (v. 1). What does it look like to come to God with care instead of just going through the motions? When do you slip into autopilot?
Verse 2 says, "So let your words be few." Why might fewer words be wiser when we speak to God? Is silence easy or hard for you?
The Teacher says God is "in heaven" and we are "on earth" (v. 2). Has God ever felt far away or silent to you? What would you honestly want to say to him about that, even if it is doubt?

A vow was a serious promise made to God, often in a hard time. Verse 5 says, "It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it." What promises do people tend to make to God when life is tough, and why is keeping our word a big deal to him?

Verse 8 says that when you see the poor oppressed, "do not be astonished at the matter." Some read this as layers of officials protecting each other, others as a hint that God is the highest watcher. How does this verse sit with you when you see injustice?
"He who loves money is never satisfied by money" (v. 10). Where have you seen wanting more take over, in others or in yourself?
"The sleep of the worker is sweet" (v. 12), but the rich man cannot sleep. What lets you rest, and what keeps you awake at night?

The Teacher says a person leaves life "naked as he arrived" (v. 15), yet calls the ability to enjoy what we have "a gift from God" (v. 19). Christians differ on whether this is real, God-given wisdom or a tired view of life without hope beyond death. How does it land for you: comforting, thin, or something else?
5.life: Start each day this week with one minute of quiet before you say anything to God. Then pick one meal or one part of your work to enjoy on purpose, and thank God for it as a gift.
5.prayer: Ask God to help you come to him with honest, unhurried words. Thank him for ordinary gifts like food, work and rest, and ask him to loosen your grip on anything you are gripping too tightly.
5.tip: The section on vows can stir up guilt in someone who has broken a promise to God. Name that gently, remind the group that God meets us with grace when we come back honestly, and keep the point on taking our words seriously rather than shaming anyone.

6.open: What is something you worked hard for and then barely got to enjoy?
questions: The Teacher describes a man who has "riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires" but is not allowed to enjoy them (v. 2). Why do you think having everything can still leave a person empty?

A hundred children and a long life were the greatest blessings in that world, yet the Teacher says they mean nothing if a person is "unsatisfied with his prosperity" (v. 3). What did people of that time prize most, and what do people around us prize today?
The Teacher says a stillborn child "has more rest than that man" (v. 5). That is a shocking thing to say. What do you think he is trying to get across, and how does it land with you?
Verse 7 says, "All a man's labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied." Where do you see that endless wanting in your own life or in the culture around you?
Verse 9 says, "Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire." What would it look like to enjoy what is actually in front of you this week?

Christians read the inability to enjoy in this chapter differently. Some see it as a moral failure like greed, and others as a mystery the Teacher simply observes without explaining. Which reading feels truer to what you have seen in real life, and why?

The chapter ends with a question: "Who knows what is good for a man during the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow?" (v. 12). If you are honest, where do you feel unsure about what is good, or about what God is doing?
The Teacher is willing to say hard things out loud and not tidy them up. What does it mean to you that the Bible includes a voice like this?
6.life: Pick one ordinary good thing this week, such as a meal, a walk or a conversation, and give it your full attention without a screen or a to-do list. Afterward, thank God for it by name.
6.prayer: Ask God for the ability to enjoy what he has given, and to trust him with the questions you cannot answer. Pray for anyone in the group who feels worn out or empty right now.
6.tip: Verses 3 to 5 about the stillborn child can be painful for anyone who has lost a baby. Read them gently, do not press people to comment on them, and remind the group that the Teacher is making a point about emptiness, not judging any child or family.

7.open: What is something you learned the hard way that you are now glad you know?
questions: The Teacher says it is better "to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting" (v. 2). Why might a funeral teach us things a party cannot? Have you ever found that to be true?
Verse 8 says, "a patient spirit is better than a proud one." Where do you find it hardest to be patient right now, and what makes it so hard?
Verse 9 warns, "Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit." What tends to set you off, and what helps you slow down before you react?
In verse 10 he says it is unwise to ask, "Why were the old days better than these?" What do we tend to miss about the present when we look back with longing?
In verse 14 he says God has made good days and hard days "along with the other," so no one can know what comes next. How does that sit with you: as a comfort, a worry, or something else?

In verse 15 he has seen "a righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness." Have you seen something like that? If you are honest, what does it stir up in you about God or about life?
Verse 20 says, "there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins." How can knowing this help us be gentler with ourselves and with others, as verses 21 and 22 suggest?
In verse 23 the Teacher says he tried to be wise, "But it was beyond me." What questions about God or life are still out of your reach? What do you do with them?
7.life: This week, when someone says something that stings, pause before you answer. Remember verse 22 and the times you have said the same kind of thing about others. Then ask God for patience and respond kindly.
7.prayer: Thank God for being wiser than we are, even when we cannot understand his ways. Ask for a patient spirit, honesty about our own faults, and peace with the questions we cannot answer.
7.tip: Verses 26 to 28 contain harsh lines about women, and some in the group may be hurt or uneasy. Say plainly that scholars are unsure whether these reflect the Teacher's bitterness, a saying he quotes, or the views of his time. Do not defend or dismiss them. Then point the group to verse 29, where he says God made all people upright and that people went after their own schemes.

8.open: What is something you have waited a long time for, and how did the waiting feel?
questions: The chapter opens with "Who is like the wise man?" (v. 1). Think of a wise person you know. What do you notice about how they carry themselves, especially under pressure?

Verse 4 says "the king's word is supreme." The writer advises patience and good timing before those in power. What do you think he is trying to protect people from, and where do you see that kind of wisdom still at work?
Verse 8 says "no one has authority over his day of death." How does it feel to be reminded of what we cannot control?
Verse 11 says when punishment is slow, "the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil." Where have you seen that happen, in the news, at work or in your own heart?
In verse 14 the writer sees "righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve." Has this ever happened to you or someone you love? What did it do to your trust in God, if anything?

Verses 12 and 13 say "it will go well with those who fear God," yet the writer still calls life unfair. Christians read these verses differently: some hear firm trust in God's justice, others hear honest doubt left open. Which sounds closer to where you are today, and why?
Verse 15 recommends joy: "eat and drink and be merry." What ordinary good things help you keep going when life does not make sense?
Verse 17 says even the wise man "is unable to comprehend" what God is doing. Is it freeing or frustrating to be told you may never have every answer? Say honestly which.
8.life: This week, choose one ordinary good gift, like a meal, a walk or time with a friend, and receive it slowly with thanks to God. If a question without an answer is weighing on you, tell God about it plainly instead of trying to solve it.
8.prayer: Thank God for the good gifts of this week. Bring the things that seem unfair or unanswered, and ask for trust and peace where understanding does not come.
8.tip: This chapter leaves hard questions open, and people may rush to tidy them up with quick answers. Let the silence sit, thank anyone who admits doubt, and remind the group that the writer himself says he could not find every answer.

9.open: What is something you put off for a long time and then finally did? How did it feel?
questions: The Teacher says "the righteous and the wise, as well as their deeds, are in God's hands" (v. 1). What does it mean to you that you cannot tell from how life goes whether you are loved or not?
Verse 2 says "There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked." Why is that so hard to accept, and when have you seen good people and bad people end up in the same place?
Verse 4 says "even a live dog is better than a dead lion." What do you think he means, and what kind of hope is he pointing to?

Verses 5 and 6 picture the dead as knowing nothing. Many readers see this as the Old Testament's limited view of death, before clearer hope of resurrection. How do you feel reading it, and what would you say to someone who finds it unsettling?
In verse 7 he says, "Go, eat your bread with joy." What ordinary pleasures do you tend to rush past or feel guilty about, and what would it look like to receive them as a gift from God?
Verse 10 says, "Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might." What is one thing in front of you right now that you could give more of yourself to?

Verse 11 says "time and chance happen to all," and verse 12 compares people to fish caught in a net. Have you ever been caught off guard by something sudden? What helped you, or what do you wish had helped?
In the story of the poor wise man, no one "remembered that poor man" (v. 15). Who have you seen do good quietly without getting credit, and what would it take to be content with that?
9.life: Pick one simple good thing this week, like a meal with someone you love or a walk, and enjoy it fully without your phone. Then pick one task you have been avoiding and give it your best effort.
9.prayer: Thank God for the gift of today and the ordinary joys in it. Ask for honesty about what you cannot control, and trust that you and the people you love are in his hands.
9.tip: Verses 2 to 10 sound bleak, and Christians read them differently: some see the Teacher's honest view of life "under the sun," others a skeptic's outlook the book later answers. Don't try to settle it. Name the disagreement, let doubters speak freely, and keep returning to the call to live gratefully and work wholeheartedly now.

10.open: What is a small mistake you made that ended up costing you more than you expected?
questions: Verse 1 says "a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor." Have you seen one small lapse overshadow a lot of good in someone's life? Did that seem fair to you?
Verse 3 says the fool "shows everyone that he is a fool" even while walking down the road. What do everyday habits reveal about a person that big moments might not?
In verse 4 the advice is to stay at your post when a ruler is angry, because "calmness lays great offenses to rest." When has staying calm helped you in a tense moment, and when has it been hard?

Verses 5 to 7 describe a world where "folly is appointed to great heights" while capable people are passed over. How do you respond when life or leadership seems upside down like this? Be as honest as you like, including any frustration or doubt.
Verses 8 to 10 talk about ordinary work that carries hidden risks, and say "skill produces success" (v. 10). What is one area of your life where a little care or preparation would save you effort?
Verse 12 says "the words of a wise man's mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool consume him." Where do your own words tend to help or hurt, at home, at work or online?
Verse 18 says "through laziness the roof caves in." What small bit of neglect, in your home, your health or your relationships, could use attention before it grows?
Verse 20 warns that private words about the powerful can get out. What does this passage suggest about how we speak of leaders, and how do you handle your frustrations with them?
10.life: Pick one small thing you have been putting off, like a repair, an apology or a habit, and deal with it this week. Notice how it feels to fix the leak before the roof caves in.
10.prayer: Ask God for wisdom in small, everyday choices and for gracious words. Thank him that he is patient with our mistakes, and pray for the leaders in your community and nation.
10.tip: Verses 8 to 11 and verse 19 are puzzling, and readers differ on exactly what they mean. Don't get stuck there. Say so briefly, then steer the group back to the clear threads: small foolishness has big effects, and wise words and steady habits matter. Also, because these are proverbs, they describe how life often goes, not guarantees, so be gentle with anyone who has suffered from a small mistake.

11.open: Do you tend to plan everything ahead of time, or do you wait and see what happens? Tell us about a time that worked out well or badly.
questions: The chapter opens with "Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again" (v. 1). Readers have long taken this as either bold business or generous giving. Which way do you hear it, and what would it look like in your life?
Verse 2 says to divide what you have among seven or even eight, "for you do not know what disaster may befall the land." What is the difference between wise preparation and fearful hoarding?
Verse 4 says, "He who watches the wind will fail to sow." Where are you waiting for perfect conditions before you begin something?

Verse 5 says we cannot understand "the work of God, the Maker of all things," any more than we know how a child is formed in the womb. How does it feel to be told you can't know everything? Is it a relief, a frustration, or something else? Be as honest as you like.
Verse 6 says, "Sow your seed in the morning, and do not rest your hands in the evening." Why might not knowing how things will turn out be a reason to keep going rather than to freeze?
Verse 7 says, "Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun." What simple good thing in your life do you most need to stop and enjoy?
Verse 8 says to rejoice in every year but to "remember the days of darkness." How can a person hold joy and a sober look at hard days together without losing either?
Verse 9 tells young people to be glad but to "know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment." What do you think it means to enjoy life while living as someone accountable to God?
11.life: Pick one thing you have been putting off because the timing never feels right, and take the first small step this week. Then pick one simple good thing, a meal, a walk, a friend, and enjoy it on purpose.
11.prayer: Thank God for the good things in your life and for holding the future when you can't. Ask for courage to act, generosity to give, and the freedom to enjoy what you have been given.
11.tip: Verse 9 is read in two ways: some take it as a real invitation to enjoy life within God's limits, others as a warning against indulgence. Say so in one sentence, don't settle it, and steer back to the chapter's bigger point about acting and enjoying life while trusting God with what you can't know. Also, verse 8 ends with "Everything to come is futile," which can sound bleak, so explain that the word means something like a breath that passes, not that life is worthless.

12.open: What is something you kept putting off that you wish you had started sooner?
questions: The Teacher says, "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth" (v. 1). Why might he say to do this early rather than later? What would the older people in the group tell their younger selves?
Verses 3 to 5 paint growing old with trembling hands, dim eyes and fading hearing. Which picture stands out to you, and how does it feel to read about aging so honestly?
Verse 7 says "the spirit returns to God who gave it." Readers differ on how much this tells us about life after death. What do you hear in that line, comfort, mystery or something else?
The Teacher ends where he began: "Futility of futilities" (v. 8). Have you ever felt that life is fleeting or hard to hold onto? You can answer honestly, even if faith feels thin right now.
Verse 11 says, "The words of the wise are like goads." A goad is a sharp stick that prods. When has a person or a piece of advice nudged you in a direction you needed but did not enjoy at the time?
Verse 12 says, "There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body." What is our version of this today, and how do we keep learning without being worn out?

Verse 13 says, "Fear God and keep His commandments." Christians differ on whether this sums up the Teacher's point or gently corrects his bleaker moments. When you hear "fear God," what do you honestly think of: awe, respect, dread, or something else?
Verse 14 says "God will bring every deed into judgment," even hidden things. Does that feel heavy, reassuring or a bit of both to you, and why?
12.life: Each day this week, spend two minutes remembering your Creator. Read verse 1 aloud, then name one good thing you received that day. Call or visit someone older and ask what they have learned about God over the years.
12.prayer: Ask God to help you give your attention now to what matters most. Pray for the older people in your life, and for anyone in the group who feels tired or unsure.
12.tip: The pictures in verses 3 to 5 are partly uncertain, so do not get stuck on what each one means. Focus on the big idea of aging and endings. Verse 14 can sound frightening, so let people say how it lands, and gently remind the group that the whole call is to remember a Creator who gave us life.
